content.heading: 5.4 Eigenvectors and Linear Transformations
content.paragraph: In this section, we will look at eigenvalues and eigenvectors of linear transformations $T:V\rightarrow V$, where $V$ is any vector space. In the case where $V$ is a finite dimensional vector space and there is a basis for $V$ consisting of eigenvectors of $T$, we will see how to represent the transformation $T$ as left multiplication by a diagonal matrix.
content.heading: Eigenvectors of Linear Transformations
content.paragraph: Previously, we looked at a variety of vector spaces including the discrete-time signal space, $\mathbb{S}$, and the set of polynomials, $\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}$. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors can be defined for linear transformations from any vector space to itself.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: Let $V$ be a vector space. An eigenvector of a linear transformation $T:V\rightarrow V$ is a nonzero vector $\textbf{x}$ in $V$ such that $T(\textbf{x}) = \text{λ}\textbf{x}$ for some scalar $\text{λ}$. A scalar $\text{λ}$ is called an eigenvalue of $T$ if there is a nontrivial solution $\textbf{x}$ of $T(\textbf{x}) = \text{λ}\textbf{x}$; such an $\textbf{x}$ is called an eigenvector corresponding to $\text{λ}$.

content.heading: The Matrix of a Linear Transformation
content.paragraph: There are branches of linear algebra that use infinite dimensional matrices to transform infinite dimensional vector spaces; however, in the remainder of this chapter we will restrict our study to linear transformations and matrices associated with finite dimensional vector spaces.

Let $V$ be an $n\text{-dimensional}$ vector space and let $T$ be any linear transformation from $V$ to $V$. To associate a matrix with $T$, choose any basis $B$ for $V$. Given any $\textbf{x}$ in $V$, the coordinate vector $\lbrack\textbf{x}\rbrack_{B}$ is in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, as is the coordinate vector of its image, $\lbrack T(\textbf{x})\rbrack_{B}$.

content.heading: Linear Transformations on ℝn
content.paragraph: In an applied problem involving $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, a linear transformation $T$ usually appears first as a matrix transformation, $\textbf{x}\mapsto\! A\textbf{x}$. If $A$ is diagonalizable, then there is a basis $B$ for $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ consisting of eigenvectors of $A$. Theorem 8 below shows that, in this case, the $B\text{-matrix}$ for $T$ is diagonal. Diagonalizing $A$ amounts to finding a diagonal matrix representation of $\textbf{x}\mapsto\! A\textbf{x}$.

note.title: Theorem ﻿8﻿
note.heading: Theorem ﻿8﻿
Diagonal Matrix Representation
note.paragraph: Suppose $A = PDP^{- 1}$, where $D$ is a diagonal $n \times n$ matrix. If $B$ is the basis for $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ formed from the columns of $P$, then $D$ is the $B\text{-matrix}$ for the transformation $\textbf{x}\mapsto\! A\textbf{x}$.

content.heading: Proof﻿
content.paragraph: Denote the columns of $P$ by $\textbf{b}_{1}\text{,}\ldots\text{,\,\,}\textbf{b}_{n}$, so that $B = \{\textbf{b}_{1},\ldots\text{,}\textbf{b}_{n}\}$ and $P = \left\lbrack {\textbf{b}_{1}\cdots\textbf{b}_{n}} \right\rbrack$. In this case, $P$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{B}$ discussed in Section 4.4, where

paragraph.math: $$\begin{array}{llll} \lbrack T\rbrack_{B} & = & \left\lbrack \left\lbrack T\left( \mathbf{b}_{1} \right) \right\rbrack_{B}~\cdots~\left\lbrack T\left( \mathbf{b}_{n} \right) \right\rbrack_{B} \right\rbrack & {\text{Definition~of}\lbrack T\rbrack_{B}} \\ & = & \left\lbrack \left\lbrack A\mathbf{b}_{1} \right\rbrack_{B}~\cdots~\left\lbrack A\mathbf{b}_{n} \right\rbrack_{B} \right\rbrack & {\text{Since}\,T\left( \mathbf{x} \right)\, = A\mathbf{x}} \\ & = & \left\lbrack P^{- 1}A\mathbf{b}_{1}~\cdots~P^{- 1}A\mathbf{b}_{n} \right\rbrack & \text{Change~of~coordinates} \\ & = & {P^{- 1}A\left\lbrack \mathbf{b}_{1}~\cdots~\mathbf{b}_{n} \right\rbrack} & \text{Matrix~multiplication} \\ & = & {P^{- 1}AP} & \end{array}$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Define $T:\text{ℝ}^{2}\rightarrow\text{ℝ}^{2}$ by $T(\textbf{x}) = A\textbf{x}$, where $A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 7 & 2 \\ {- 4} & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$. Find a basis $B$ for $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ with the property that the $B\text{-matrix}$ for $T$ is a diagonal matrix.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: From Example 2 in Section 5.3, we know that $A = PDP^{- 1}$, where

The columns of $P$, call them $\textbf{b}_{1}$ and $\textbf{b}_{2}$, are eigenvectors of $A$. By Theorem 8, $D$ is the $B\text{-matrix}$ for $T$ when $B = \{\textbf{b}_{1},\textbf{b}_{2}\}$. The mappings $\textbf{x}\mapsto\! A\textbf{x}$ and $\textbf{u}\mapsto\! D\textbf{u}$ describe the same linear transformation, relative to different bases.

content.heading: Similarity of Matrix Representations
content.paragraph: The proof of Theorem 8 did not use the information that $D$ was diagonal. Hence, if $A$ is similar to a matrix $C$, with $A = PCP^{- 1}$, then $C$ is the $B\text{-matrix}$ for the transformation $\textbf{x}\mapsto\! A\textbf{x}$ when the basis $B$ is formed from the columns of $P$. The factorization $A = PCP^{- 1}$ is shown in Figure 4.

figure.label: Figure 4
figure.caption: Similarity of two matrix representations: A = PCP-1

image.alt: A figure shows four arrows forming a rectangle with matrix notations on its vertices.

content.paragraph: Conversely, if $T:\text{ℝ}^{n}\rightarrow\text{ℝ}^{n}$ is defined by $T(\textbf{x}) = A\textbf{x}$, and if $B$ is any basis for $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, then the $B\text{-matrix}$ for $T$ is similar to $A$. In fact, the calculations in the proof of Theorem 8 show that if $P$ is the matrix whose columns come from the vectors in $B$, then $\lbrack T\rbrack_{B} = P^{- 1}AP$. This important connection between the matrix of a linear transformation and similar matrices is highlighted here.

note.paragraph: The set of all matrices similar to a matrix $A$ coincides with the set of all matrix representations of the transformation $\textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x}$.
